1. Model consistently overestimates prices in early forecast periods, especially after sharp spikes or volatility events — adjust downward by 5–10% for the first 5–7 days post-event.

2. Forecast mean tends to be higher than true mean, especially in high-volatility periods — apply a 3–5% downward bias to the average forecast for 30-day windows with >10% standard deviation.

3. Model exhibits “overshoot” after price spikes — if forecast rises >15% above recent 7-day average, reduce by 10–15% to avoid overcorrection.

4. Model underestimates prices during prolonged downward trends — if true outcome drops below 30% of 30-day moving average, increase forecast by 5–8% to avoid underreaction.

5. Forecast lags true price movements by 2–5 days — adjust forecast to align with 3-day moving average of true values for lag correction.

6. Model fails to capture sudden reversals — if true outcome shows a sharp reversal (e.g., >15% drop in 3 days), reduce forecast by 5–10% for next 3–5 days to avoid overconfidence in continuation.

7. In low-volatility periods, model tends to over-smooth — increase forecast variance by 1–2% to reflect market uncertainty.

8. Model underestimates price during “recovery” phases after crashes — if true outcome rises >5% from 30-day low, increase forecast by 3–7% to avoid underestimating momentum.
